links.outcome: Radiologist diagnostic accuracy with vs without GPT-5 assistance
links.effect: R1/R2 accuracy rose from 73%/71% unassisted to 87%/86% with browser GPT-5 and 94%/94% with optimal-settings GPT-5 (P=0.001; P=0.031/0.028). Overreliance not assessed.
links.quote: With browser-based GPT-5 assistance, their accuracy significantly improved to 87% (75/86; 95% CI: 79%–94%) and 86% (74/86; 95% CI: 78%–93%), respectively ( P = 0.001, P = 0.001).

links.outcome: Clinician performance with AI assistance versus unassisted in the workflow, not standalone metrics
links.effect: Radiologists' accuracy improved with GPT-5 assistance (73%/71% to 87%/86% to 94%); differential Likert scores improved to 4.56 and 4.49; assisted juniors outperformed the abdominal radiologist on differentials.
links.quote: Using GPT-5 with the optimal settings further improved their accuracy to 94% (81/86; 95% CI: 88%–99%) ( P = 0.031, P = 0.028).

links.outcome: GPT-5 performance across input formats, temperature/top-p settings, and repeat-run reproducibility
links.effect: Accuracy 12% image-only vs 58% with text; 53% to 73% across temperatures; Round 2 agreement kappa 0.882 for diagnosis, no significant difference (P=0.41). Temperature 2 outputs were unevaluable.
links.quote: Agreement between GPT-5 responses generated with the optimal settings at baseline and in the Round 2 evaluation was high, with Cohen’s κ: 0.882 (95% CI: 0.80–0.96) for the most likely diagnosis and κ: 0.816 for differential diagnosis performance, indicating strong agreement.

links.outcome: GPT-5 and GPT-5-assisted radiologists compared against unassisted and expert abdominal radiologist
links.effect: Abdominal radiologist accuracy 92% exceeded unassisted juniors (P<0.001) but did not differ from assisted juniors; assisted juniors outperformed the abdominal radiologist on differentials (P=0.002, 0.001).
links.quote: Comparatively, AR achieved an accuracy of 92% (79/86; 95% CI: 85%–97%), which was superior to the accuracy of R1 and R2 without GPT-5 assistance ( P < 0.001) but not significantly different from their performances with both browser-based GPT-5 and GPT-5 with the optimal settings ( Table 4 ).

links.outcome: Data contamination and generalizability from a single open-access dataset
links.effect: Single open-access dataset raises contamination concerns; near-exact reference phrasing overlap in 2/86 cases (2.3%); no real patient data used.
links.quote: First, it was based on a single open-access dataset, which raises concerns about data contamination and limits the generalizability of the results to the broader, heterogeneous patient populations encountered in actual radiologic practice.

links.outcome: Model changes over time and undocumented browser settings affecting performance
links.effect: Authors note browser GPT-5 responses reflect a point in time; stochasticity and updates or undocumented internal configuration may cause performance differences at different times.
links.quote: Therefore, the browser-based GPT-5 responses included in the study reflect the responses at the time of the study.

models_evaluated: GPT-5 via OpenAI API with temperature/top-p settings

links.outcome: accuracy with clinical context inputs
links.effect: Accuracy increased from 12% to 58% when imaging findings and clinical presentation were added; P<0.001.
links.quote: With the "only visual" input format, browser-based GPT-5 achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 12%, increasing to 58% when imaging findings and clinical presentations were provided (P < 0.001).

links.outcome: accuracy across hyperparameter settings
links.effect: Optimal temperature 1.5/top-p 1 raised accuracy to 73%; mean differential score improved from 3.44 to 3.84.
links.quote: Hyperparameter optimization further improved GPT-5 performance, with diagnostic accuracy increasing to 73% at the optimal settings (temperature: 1.5, top-p: 1) and mean differential diagnosis scores improving from 3.44 to 3.84.

links.outcome: repeat-run reproducibility
links.effect: Round 2 agreement was high: diagnosis κ 0.882 (95% CI: 0.80–0.96); differential κ 0.816.
links.quote: Agreement between GPT-5 responses generated with the optimal settings at baseline and in the Round 2 evaluation was high, with Cohen’s κ: 0.882 (95% CI: 0.80–0.96) for the most likely diagnosis and κ: 0.816 for differential diagnosis performance, indicating strong agreement.

links.outcome: radiologist accuracy with AI assistance
links.effect: Accuracy improved from 73%/71% unaided to 87%/86% with browser assistance and 94%/94% with optimized assistance.
links.quote: Radiologist accuracy improved from 73%/71% unaided to 87%/86% with browser-based assistance and to 94%/94% with optimized assistance, approaching the AR benchmark (92%).

links.outcome: standalone GPT-5 diagnostic accuracy
links.effect: Standalone GPT-5 accuracy ranged from 53% (46/86) to 73% (63/86) across temperature settings.
links.quote: At temperature settings of 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5, diagnostic accuracies were 53% (46/86; 95% CI: 42%–63%), 64% (55/86; 95% CI: 54%–74%), 66% (57/86; 95% CI: 56%–76%), and 73% (63/86; 95% CI: 63%–82%), respectively.

links.outcome: radiologist diagnostic accuracy with versus without AI assistance
links.effect: Radiologist accuracy increased from 73% and 71% unaided to 87% and 86% with browser-based assistance and 94% with optimal assistance, demonstrating standalone AI accuracy (58% and 73%) failed to predict human-AI performance.
links.quote: The radiologists' diagnostic accuracy increased from 73% and 71% without assistance to 87% and 86% with browser-based GPT-5 assistance and further to 94% with GPT-5 with optimal settings assistance.

links.outcome: GPT-5 response reproducibility across repeated runs
links.effect: Agreement between baseline and Round 2 was high (Cohen's kappa 0.882 for most likely diagnosis; kappa 0.816 for differential diagnosis), indicating strong agreement and response stability.
links.quote: Agreement between GPT-5 responses generated with the optimal settings at baseline and in the Round 2 evaluation was high, with Cohen’s κ: 0.882 (95% CI: 0.80–0.96) for the most likely diagnosis and κ: 0.816 for differential diagnosis performance, indicating strong agreement.

links.outcome: diagnostic accuracy with visual-only versus multimodal input
links.effect: Browser-based GPT-5 achieved diagnostic accuracy of only 12% (10/86; 95% CI: 6%-21%) with visual-only input, compared to 58% when clinical presentation and imaging findings were added.
links.quote: Browser-based GPT-5 demonstrated limited diagnostic accuracy in the “only visual” format, correctly answering 12% of cases [10/86; 95% confidence interval (CI), 6%–21%].
